name: Aoraki/Mount Cook
info_ref: File BRD-02-02-00-07; Objective folder ID: fA325625; 2023 346-2 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482801, A4869760}
info_origin: [See Kā Huru Manu, Ngāi Tahu's cultural heritage atlas, for more details](http://www.kahurumanu.co.nz/atlas?find={e36db1e3-3d52-e311-8212-005056970030}); [See entry in the dictionary of New Zealand Biography for James Cook](https://teara.govt.nz/en/biographies/1c25/cook-james); .; 'The name Aoraki is also found in other parts of the country and the Pacific (such as the mountain Aora’i in Tahiti). Two traditions are related to the naming of this, New Zealand’s highest mountain. The first relates the wreckage of the Āraiteuru waka at Matakaea (Shag Point). After capsizing, many of the passengers went ashore to explore the land, including Kirikirikatata who carried his grandson Aoraki on his shoulders. The travellers needed to be back at the waka before daylight, but most did not make it, instead turning into many of the well-known landmarks of Te Waipounamu; Aoraki, being on his grandfather’s shoulders, was the tallest. In the second tradition Aoraki was an atua (god) who descended from the heavens with his brothers; attempting the return voyage their waka crashed into the Pacific Ocean forming what would later be known as the South Island (Te Waka-o-Aoraki). Aoraki and his brothers climbed to the highest side of the waka where they turned into the highest peaks of the Southern Alps. Despite the association of the English name with Captain James Cook, he did not actually see the peak when sailing up the west coast of the South Island in 1770. The mountain did not take an English name until 1851, when Captain John Lort Stokes of the survey ship HMS Acheron christened it after the famous explorer. The current dual name dates from the 1998 Ngāi Tahu Claims Settlement Act, and is also the name of the national park.’ Source: Dowling, Peter & A.W. Reed, New Zealand Place Names, 2025.
info_description: Feature shown on: NZMS260-H36 793308; Infomap 346-02 Te Wai Pounamu Edition 1 1995; NZTopo50-BX15 693691

name: Mount Erebus
info_origin: Discovered and named by Ross on 28 January 1841 for the 370 ton vessel from which he discovered the volcano. It is the loftiest active volcano in the Antarctic. The first ascent was by a party under David in 1908, and the second by a party under Priestley in 1912. The climb presented little difficulty, and in 1912 sledges were pulled to a height of about 2743m.
info_description: An active volcano, 3790m high, which forms the summit of Ross Island. Feature depicted on: NZ AntTopo50-ME14

name: Whakaari / White Island
info_ref: Mins v/2 49/52, 6/53; Corres XXVII pp 193, 252, 270, 278, XXVIII pp 20-25, 50, 57, 93, 284; File BRD/02/01/00/14; Objective folder ID: fA325625; Dual name standardisation: Objective IDs: A4405369, A4507521; 2023 346-1 edition two: {Objective IDs: fA482800, A5013544}
info_origin: Whakaari means to make visible". When Ngātoroirangi was freezing to death on Mount Tongariro he called upon his sisters Kuiwai and Haungaroa in Hawaiiki for help. They dispatched two fire taniwha which travelled swiftly under the sea and ground. The spirits surfaced several times to to check where they were going, one spot being offshore, forming Whakaari/White Island. The name White Island was given by Lieutenant Cook on account of the dense clouds of white steam emitted. The feature is named Isle of Wight and Isle of White on some manuscript charts, giving the name a double meaning by reference to the island off the south coast of England. See [history relating to Cook's place names](https://earth.google.com/web/data=Mj8KPQo7CiExMjJfZ1puZmJFV2hFRFlvSFVNVG5YU05CRWZTYTBfSWoSFgoUMDc1NkI1MTJFNjBGRjk5NTA2RDg)"
info_description: Active marine volcano in the Bay of Plenty. Feature shown on: NZTopo50-BC40 698391
info_note: Meaning of Whakaari "exposed to view (visible plume of steam)" Sourced from Infomap 346-01 Te Ika a Māui Edition 1 1995 Change from White Island (Whakaari) [as shown on maps] Published on [346-01 edition 2 (2023) – Te Ika-a-Māui](https://www.linz.govt.nz/resources/guide/te-ika-maui-tangata-whenua-place-names-map): "the fire spirits Pupū and Te Hōata were sent from Hawaiki to save Ngātoroirangi from freezing on Tongariro and surfaced here to check where they were going"
